item.title: Redwoods, Coast, and Cabernet
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

Tracing Northern California’s dramatic transitions from vine to coast.

Drive thirty minutes west of the Napa Valley floor, and the tidy, sun-drenched grid of cabernet vines gives way to something far raw: dense stands of old-growth redwoods, fog-draped ridges, and the craggy, tide-swept cliffs of the Sonoma Coast. While most visitors treat wine country as a series of stationary tastings, the region is fundamentally defined by these sudden, stark shifts in terrain—best experienced from behind the wheel on a loop through its backroads.

Starting at the southern nexus of Napa and Sonoma, a drive up the historic Silverado Trail offers a quiet alternative to Highway 29. Lined with oak trees and stone-built estates, this two-lane corridor bypasses central valley traffic, connecting rustic tasting rooms in Rutherford with the hot springs and volcanic foothills of Calistoga.

From the valley’s northern tip, a western cut across the Mayacamas Mountains shifts the scenery entirely. As the pavement winds down toward Bodega Bay, the warm air of the valley vanishes, replaced by cool ocean breezes and sweeping Pacific vistas. Further inland, the route dips beneath the towering, light-dappled canopy of Sonoma’s redwood groves, where narrow roads twist through giant sequoias before looping back toward the vines.

Local resorts like Carneros Resort and Spa cater directly to this road-trip culture, offering curated routing guides and vintage or electric vehicle rentals for guests using the property as a regional launchpad. But whether behind the wheel of a classic convertible or a local rental, navigating these interconnected loops proves that Northern California’s true allure lies in the vivid landscapes between the destinations.

item.title: Two Hyatt Culinary Leaders Bring Global Experience to Bali’s Sanur
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hyatt Regency Bali and Andaz Bali, by Hyatt are entering a new chapter for their food and beverage programs with the appointment of Ivan Gutierrez as Cluster Director of Food & Beverage and Chef Vincenzo Gatti as Cluster Executive Chef. Together, the two leaders bring extensive experience across Hyatt properties in Asia, including Park Hyatt Tokyo, Grand Hyatt Tokyo, Grand Hyatt Seoul and Hyatt Regency Hua Hin, giving the two Sanur resorts a leadership team with a distinctly international perspective on dining and hospitality.

Chef Vincenzo arrives in Bali after serving as Executive Chef at Andaz Pattaya Jomtien Beach, where La Cucina Italian Restaurant and Fish Club Seafood Restaurant received Michelin Guide recognition when the guide launched its Pattaya selection in 2025. Gutierrez, meanwhile, most recently led food and beverage at Grand Hyatt Erawan Bangkok and has held leadership roles across Hyatt properties in Japan, China and Thailand. In their new roles, Gutierrez will oversee food and beverage strategy and service culture across both resorts, while Gatti will lead the culinary direction, with both emphasizing collaboration, talent development and memorable guest experiences.

The Curated Take: The appointments point to an increasingly sophisticated culinary identity for Sanur, where international hospitality expertise can intersect with Bali’s distinctive sense of place. The more interesting question is not simply what new restaurants or menus might emerge, but how these two leaders translate experience gathered across Asia into dining that feels appropriate to Bali and its guests.

item.title: Bellevue Builds a Car-Free Basecamp for Pacific Northwest Adventures
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Bellevue, Washington, is making it easier to experience the Pacific Northwest without a car, with a growing network of shuttles, light rail connections and bike options linking travelers from arrival to outdoor adventure. The expanded Bellevue Airport & Cruise Shuttle connects hotels with Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and Seattle’s cruise terminals, while the new Bellevue Light Rail Shuttle provides free, on-demand electric transportation from the Bellevue Downtown Station to hotels, restaurants, shops and attractions. Ride Bellevue adds another layer, giving visitors access to e-bikes as well as gravel and mountain bikes for exploring the region without bringing their own equipment.

The transportation changes arrive as Bellevue adds new reasons to make the city a base for a Pacific Northwest trip. Nobu Bellevue and Nobu Bellevue Residences are planned for 2027, alongside The Emily Hotel and a new winter festival centered on light, art and seasonal programming. In the Wilburton district, the evolving Eastrail corridor and restoration of the historic Wilburton Trestle will connect visitors to a growing regional trail network. With more than 100 parks and public spaces, Lake Washington shoreline and easy connections to Seattle, Woodinville Wine Country and mountain recreation, Bellevue is positioning itself as a place where urban comfort and the outdoors can be part of the same itinerary.

The Curated Take: Bellevue’s most interesting development may be the connective tissue between its experiences. Rather than requiring travelers to choose between a polished urban stay and access to the Pacific Northwest landscape, the city is building a model around both. For travelers who prefer the ease of a sophisticated home base but still want nature, culture and regional exploration within reach, that changes how Bellevue fits into a Seattle-area itinerary.

item.title: Dunedin and Waitaki Bring New Zealand’s Quirky Side Into Focus
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Dunedin and Waitaki have been named among Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel destinations for 2027, putting one of New Zealand’s most distinctive regional pairings on the global travel map. The only New Zealand destination included in the 2027 edition, the area joins 50 destinations worldwide recognized by the travel guide for the year ahead. Lonely Planet describes Dunedin and nearby Ōamaru as among Aotearoa’s “coolest and quirkiest” corners, where Victorian heritage, creative culture, dramatic coastal landscapes and wildlife come together in unexpected ways.

The character of the region is perhaps best understood through its contrasts. In Dunedin, travelers can move from its arts, restaurant and cocktail scene into green hills, coastal bays and wildlife experiences, while Ōamaru adds its distinctive Victorian whitestone architecture, Steampunk culture and nightly little blue penguin sightings. The wider Waitaki region extends the story into lakes, rivers, open landscapes and the Waitaki Whitestone UNESCO Global Geopark, creating a destination that feels less like a collection of attractions and more like a place with its own unmistakable personality.

The Curated Take: Lonely Planet’s recognition is particularly fitting because Dunedin and Waitaki’s appeal is not built around a single headline attraction. It is the unusual combination of heritage, landscape, wildlife and local creativity that gives the region its identity. For travelers looking beyond New Zealand’s most familiar routes, this is a part of the South Island where the unexpected is part of the experience.

item.title: Four Seasons Singapore Creates a Private Enclave for Multigenerational Stays
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Four Seasons Hotel Singapore has introduced a new Three-Bedroom Premier Suite designed to give families and friends the ability to travel together without giving up personal space. Set along tree-lined Orchard Boulevard, the 180-square-metre residential-style suite has its own private entrance and discreet corridor that can be closed off to connect the Premier Suite with two additional guest rooms, creating a private three-bedroom enclave. Separate bedrooms and marble bathrooms provide individual retreat spaces, while a generous living area, private bar and flexible dining and workspace create room for everyone to gather.

The suite is designed particularly with multigenerational holidays, celebrations and longer stays in mind, complementing Four Seasons Singapore’s broader collection of 41 suites. Guests can move from their private enclave to the hotel’s dining and wellness offerings, including Cantonese cuisine at Jiang-Nan Chun, Japanese-Peruvian dining at Nobu Singapore and botanical-inspired experiences at One-Ninety. The Four Seasons Spa and Chi Longevity Clinic add further options for relaxation and personalized wellbeing, while the hotel’s location places guests near Orchard Road and Singapore Botanic Gardens.

The Curated Take: The suite reflects a shift in how luxury families are traveling. The goal is no longer simply to provide a larger room, but to create a private residential environment that allows different generations or groups of friends to share a trip while maintaining independence. That combination of togetherness and personal space is particularly relevant to longer, experience-led stays where the accommodation becomes part of the destination experience.

item.title: W Bali Reimagines the Seminyak Beach Club Experience With Alunê
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
W Bali – Seminyak has introduced Alunê, a new beachfront destination occupying the former Woobar footprint and designed around the natural rhythm of Seminyak’s shoreline. Its name draws from the Indonesian alunan, referring to the flowing rhythm of waves and sound, combined with the French lune, or moon. That idea carries through the design, which takes its cues from the beach’s southwest-facing sunsets with wave-inspired forms, oceanic colors and a bar backed by illuminated mosaic and amber glass that echoes the changing light outside.

The experience shifts naturally from daytime to evening, with chef-driven coastal dishes, locally inspired ingredients, wellness-focused frozen bowls and a sunset ritual built around cocktails and live music. Private pool cabanas with jacuzzis offer a more secluded alternative to the club’s social spaces, while the launch of Club Lacoste adds padel and a wellness-oriented dimension to the resort’s beachfront offering. Together, the two concepts create a broader day-to-night experience, allowing guests to move from an active afternoon on the court to dining, music and sunset on the same stretch of Seminyak shore.

The Curated Take: Alunê is interesting because it treats the beachfront as more than a setting for a conventional beach club. The concept is built around the actual rhythm of Seminyak, from its southwest sunset to the movement between activity, socializing and downtime. Paired with Club Lacoste, it reflects a broader evolution in resort culture where sport, wellness, food and nightlife increasingly overlap rather than occupying separate parts of the guest experience.

item.title: Walking the Earth's Living Archives
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Pilgrimage, tide, and trade across three ancient landscapes where the soil remembers what humans forget.

Long before humans carved the first stone pillars or drew borders across maps, the physical Earth was already recording our presence. We tend to view history as something housed in libraries, museum display cases, or ruined stone temples. Yet the most enduring archives are not built by human hands; they are written directly into moss, mud, volcanic ash, and deep oceanic trenches.

To travel through a sacred topography is to step out of linear time and into geography shaped by centuries of movement, ritual, and survival. Across Japan’s mist-shrouded peninsula, Denmark’s shifting intertidal flats, and Indonesia’s isolated volcanic islands, the landscape does not merely host the journey—it is the story itself.

Part I: The Mountain & The Pilgrim’s Path

On the Kii Peninsula of Japan, the ancient trails of the Kumano Kodo wind through forests of towering Japanese cedar (sugi) that have stood watch over seekers for more than a thousand years. Here, Shinto animism and Buddhist practice merge seamlessly into the terrain. Mountains, rivers, and waterfalls are not scenic backdrops; they are kami—divine spirits inhabiting the natural world.

To walk these paths—ascending the moss-draped stone staircases of Daidoko-zaka—is an act of active devotion. Rain filters through a thick canopy, carrying the damp, earthen scent of soil settled by the footsteps of medieval emperors, samurai, and modern wanderers. Small stone Jizo statues, draped in faded red bibs and weathered by centuries of mountain mist, guard quiet turns in the trail. As the distant roar of Nachi Falls echoes through the valley, the topography reveals its fundamental truth: the trail is not merely a route to a sacred destination, but the prayer itself.

Part II: The Tidal Archive & Rhythms of Survival

Far to the west, along the coast of Denmark, history is written not in stone, but in water and sand. The Wadden Sea represents the world’s largest unbroken system of intertidal mudflats and barrier islands—a landscape defined entirely by transience. Twice a day, the North Sea retreats to reveal vast stretches of exposed seabed, reshaping the horizon with every turning tide.

For millennia, human survival along these shores has been governed by this natural pulse. During low tide, travelers set out on foot across the sea floor—a practice known as wadlopen—where every step crunches over cockle shells and cold, mineral-rich mud. High above, millions of migratory shorebirds fill the wide skies of Ho Bay, tracing aerial flyways as ancient as the coastline itself. In a world increasingly obsessed with permanent structures, the Wadden Sea hums with a quieter wisdom: that heritage can be fluid, fleeting, and reborn with every wave.

Part III: The Maritime Crucible

Rising abruptly from the 4,000-meter abyssal depths of the Banda Sea, the tiny, volcanic specks of Indonesia’s Spice Islands feel impossibly remote. Yet these isolated landmasses—dominated by the dark, looming peak of Gunung Api—once stood at the very center of global geopolitical history as the world’s sole origin of nutmeg and mace.

Navigating these deep waters aboard expedition itineraries with operators like Rainforest Cruises connects travelers to centuries of Austronesian seafaring and the turbulent tides of global trade aboard traditional wooden schooners. On shore, black volcanic sand beaches give way to groves where the scent of wild nutmeg dries in the warm equatorial air. Beneath the glass-clear surface, pristine coral gardens flourish in the shadow of ancient trade routes. The islands carry the weight of a complex, multi-layered past, offering proof that even the smallest, most isolated topographies can alter the course of human civilization.

The Earth as Memory

Whether ascending a misty mountain pass, walking a seabed exposed by the moon, or sailing toward a volcanic shore, these places demand a slower, more deliberate kind of attention. They remind us that we are not the first to pass through, nor will we be the last. As long as humans seek meaning in the world around them, the story continues—written continuously into the living fabric of the Earth.

item.title: The Red Centre Turns Art Into a Way of Experiencing Country
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Central Australia’s Red Centre has been named among Lonely Planet’s World’s Top 25 Experiences Hotlist for 2027, with its immersive art experiences earning the region a place on the global list. The recognition highlights a creative landscape that extends well beyond traditional galleries, from Aboriginal art centres and contemporary artists to outdoor painting and large-scale installations across the desert. In Alice Springs, Parrtjima transforms Mparntwe through light, art and storytelling, while Iltja Ntjarra (Many Hands) Art Centre offers visitors the opportunity to see Western Arrernte artists working in the tradition of Albert Namatjira.

Further into the Red Centre, art becomes inseparable from the landscape itself. Wintjiri Wiru uses drones, light and sound to share Anangu stories against the backdrop of Uluru, while Sunrise Journeys projects art and stories across the desert at dawn. Bruce Munro’s Field of Light at Uluru and Light Towers at Kings Canyon create another interpretation of the desert after dark, while Art Tours of Australia leads small-group watercolour sessions in the Tjoritja (West MacDonnell Ranges). Together, these experiences offer travelers different ways to encounter Central Australia’s creativity while gaining a deeper understanding of Country, culture and the region’s Traditional Custodians.

The Curated Take: What makes the Red Centre particularly compelling is that art is not confined to a designated cultural stop. It can emerge from an artist working in an art centre, a story carried through light and sound, or the act of sitting outdoors and painting the landscape itself. That makes art a pathway into understanding place, rather than simply another attraction to add to an itinerary.

item.title: Sydney Harbour Sets the Stage for a Summer on the Water and Vivid Sydney
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Sydney Harbour takes on an even bigger role in the city’s summer travel season as Captain Cook Cruises extends its sightseeing and Taronga Zoo experiences through March 2027. Options include harbour cruises between Circular Quay and Manly, hop-on, hop-off itineraries linking waterfront destinations such as Taronga Zoo, Shark Island and Manly Beach, and combined cruise-and-zoo experiences. The range gives visitors different ways to experience Sydney from the water, whether spending a full day moving between harbour landmarks or simply taking in the skyline from the deck.

Looking ahead to Vivid Sydney 2027, Captain Cook Cruises is also introducing dining experiences aboard Sydney 2000 during the festival, including multi-course à la carte and degustation menus. Selected evening cruises will combine dinner with views of Sydney’s illuminated waterfront, while participating vessels will themselves become part of the festival through official Vivid Sydney light installations. With the city transformed after dark, a harbour cruise offers a different perspective on the festival, shifting the experience from navigating the crowds along the foreshore to watching Sydney’s landmarks and illuminated precincts unfold from the water.

The Curated Take: Sydney Harbour is often treated as something travelers see rather than something they experience. These offerings make the water itself the itinerary, whether that means using the harbour as a way to explore the city during summer or turning it into a front-row seat for Vivid. For a destination already defined by its waterfront, that shift in perspective can make a familiar Sydney experience feel new.

item.title: Highway 101 Turns 100 With a New Central California Road Trip
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
As California’s Highway 101 approaches its 100th anniversary this November, Nomada Hotel Group is using the milestone to trace a contemporary road trip through the Central Coast. The route connects five historic and design-focused properties between the Santa Ynez Valley, San Luis Obispo and Paso Robles, linking wine country with coastal communities and historic roadside towns. Rather than treating the highway simply as a way to get from one destination to another, the journey highlights the distinctive character of the communities along the route.

The road trip also points toward the next chapter of Central California’s roadside culture. Nomada plans to add Pozo in summer 2027, transforming the historic Pozo Saloon, which has welcomed travelers since 1858, into a small encampo retreat with vintage Airstreams and spaces for vans and RVs. Set near a lake, hiking and horseback riding trails, the property will add a more deliberately rustic stop to the collection while preserving the saloon’s longstanding role as a gathering place for the community. Together, the existing hotels and forthcoming Pozo property suggest a version of the California road trip built around character, history and places worth slowing down for.

The Curated Take: The centennial provides a useful reminder that the best road trips are rarely about the road itself. Highway 101 has spent a century connecting California communities, and Nomada’s approach gives travelers reasons to experience those connections through historic properties, wine country and unexpected roadside places. It is a more experiential interpretation of the classic American road trip, where the stops become as important as the drive.
